newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin trumpets Russia's young, promotes reformer.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin trumpets Russia's young, promotes reformer.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, vowing to leave power in the hands of a new generation when he steps down, put young reformer Boris Nemtsov in charge of Russia's vital fuel and energy sector on Thursday.
Nemtsov, 37, will take on the role of Fuel and Energy Minister in addition to the post he has held since last month as one of two first deputy prime ministers.

The appointment confirms the boyish-looking Nemtsov as one of Russia's most powerful politicians and boosts his image as a potential presidential candidate in the year 2000, when Yeltsin's second term as president is due to end.

The appointment was a new warning to seasoned Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who has seen control of economic reforms shift away from him under a government reshuffle and whose hopes of succeeding Yeltsin appear to be receding.

"I am convinced that today we should more boldly promote young people to responsible positions of leadership. People want to see young faces, want to trust young people more, to count more on them," Yeltsin said in his regular radio address.

"I am addressing the chairman of the government, Viktor Stepanovich Chernomyrdin, the head of the presidential administration, ministers, governors, city mayors, all officials -- show more daring in drawing young people into the work!"

The Kremlin announced Nemtsov's appointment soon after Yeltsin and the presidents of China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan had signed a treaty intended to end the risk of confrontation on the former Soviet-Chinese border.
The treaty, signed in the Kremlin, set out plans for troop reductions along the long border which they hope will set an example to others on how to maintain regional security.
Yeltsin, whose health is a major political concern after his heart surgery last November and pneumonia in January, said he was looking ahead to the end of his four-year term.
"I am already 66. Three years remain before my term of presidency runs out and I must prove my worth during these remaining three years," he said.
"I hope to hand over power to younger successors, so that they could continue what we have begun."

The words must have been music to the ears of Nemtsov who has established himself as a leading presidential candidate in a matter of weeks since being brought into the Kremlin from the governorship of the Nizhny Novgorod region southeast of Moscow.

Alongside first deputy prime minister Anatoly Chubais, Nemtsov has been given a huge role and a high profile in putting economic reforms back on track under a reshuffle which has brought younger and more liberal politicians to the top.

Nemtsov is in charge of breaking down natural monopolies in spheres such as gas, electricity and railways and housing reform and now gains sway over Chernomyrdin's fiefdom in the energy sector, which has immense political and economic importance.

Chernomyrdin, 59, the former head of the natural gas monopoly Gazprom, suffered his latest humiliation of recent weeks at the hands of Yeltsin, whom he has served loyally as prime minister since December 1992.
Yeltsin admonished him for failing to complete the reshuffle several weeks after it began under the Kremlin leader's orders.
"Is it that we lack personnel? I will never believe that. We have personnel. It is simply that we are afraid of promoting young people," he said.

"Yes, we are afraid, Viktor Stepanovich. Don't worry, they will not aim at unseating you. They are too busy to engage in intrigues, to whisper in ears, to engage in bureaucratic infighting. They are coming to do a job."

Some political analysts say Chernomyrdin has become just a figurehead leader. Others say he could rebound if powerful industrialists resist reforms and Nemtsov fails to revitalise the reform process. They say the premier may still hope to run for president.
